title: Three-Dimensional Trunk–Pelvis Kinematics During Cross-Court and Long-Line Table Tennis Strokes: A Statistical Parametric Mapping Analysis
content: Stroke direction in table tennis may require technique-specific adaptations of trunk–pelvis motion, but the timing and magnitude of these adjustments remain unclear. This study compared cross-court (CC) and long-line (LL) kinematics during forehand counter-topspin (F_FH), forehand topspin (TP_FH), and backhand topspin (TP_BH). Ten high-level players performed both target directions while whole-body kinematics were recorded using a 16-sensor inertial measurement unit system. A total of 580 valid strokes were analysed. Continuous torso–pelvis flexion–extension, lateral bending, and axial rotation trajectories were compared using one-dimensional statistical parametric mapping (SPM), while discrete variables were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction. CC and LL trajectories were largely similar across techniques; only a late follow-through axial-rotation difference was identified for TP_BH (SPM cluster, p = 0.030). Discrete analyses revealed technique-specific differences in selected contact angles, ranges of motion, trunk–pelvis separation measures, and angular velocities, with predominantly negligible-to-small effect sizes and no variable differentiating all three techniques. Stroke direction therefore appears to be accommodated mainly through brief, technique-specific kinematic adjustments rather than a global alteration of torso–pelvis movement patterns, highlighting the complementary information provided by continuous and discrete biomechanical analyses.
